subject: ENGLISH LANGUAGE
title: Grammar in Use: Language Patterns (Interrogatives)
overview: Interrogatives are words we use to ask questions. In this sub-strand you will find who, what, where, when and whose in texts about sport, build questions with them, and answer those questions clearly. Asking well helps you learn rules, find lost kit and talk about your favourite game.

lessons.title: Spotting who, what, where, when and whose
objectives: Name five interrogatives and the kind of answer each one seeks.
Find them in questions about sport.
Explain why questions matter in communication.
lessons.intro: A teammate says, 'The match is ready.' You still do not know the place or the time. One well-chosen question fills the gap. The first word of that question tells everyone what kind of answer you need.
lessons.notes:
### Five interrogatives
An interrogative is a question word. In this sub-strand we use five:

- who asks about a person
- what asks about a thing, an idea or an action
- where asks about a place
- when asks about a time
- whose asks about an owner

Look at these questions from a games lesson.

Who is the captain? (a person)
What is in the kit bag? (a thing)
Where is the field? (a place)
When does the race start? (a time)
Whose whistle is on the desk? (an owner)

Each question ends with a question mark. The interrogative usually comes first.

### Find them in a short text
Our coach asked us five questions before the match. Who will lead the team? What must we carry? Where shall we meet? When will the referee blow the whistle? Whose name is first on the list? We could not start until those answers were clear.

If you cover the question word, the rest of the sentence no longer tells you what is being asked. That is how you test that the word is doing the work.

### Why we ask
Questions help us learn, check a fact and include other people. A player who asks when the practice is will not arrive late. A player who asks whose bottle this is will not take the wrong one. A class that can ask clear questions understands the game more quickly. Interrogatives make those questions precise, so the answer can be precise too.

keyWords.meaning: a word used to ask a question, such as who, what, where, when or whose
the sign ? that comes at the end of a question

examples.problem: Name the interrogative and say what it asks for: Where do we practise on Friday?
steps: The question word is at the beginning.
Where always asks for a place.
examples.answer: Where. It asks for a place.

examples.problem: Which interrogative fits? ______ shoes are under the bench?
steps: The question is about an owner, not a place or a time.
Whose asks about an owner.

activity.title: Mark the question words
materials: A newspaper, magazine, brochure or textbook page
steps: In pairs, read a short sports report, a school notice or a page your teacher provides.
Underline every who, what, where, when and whose you find.
Beside each one, write person, thing, place, time or owner.
If the page has no questions, turn three statements into questions and mark the new interrogatives.

practice.question: Match each word to what it asks: who, where, when, whose.
practice.answer: who — a person; where — a place; when — a time; whose — an owner.

practice.question: Underline the interrogative: What did the coach say about fair play?
Why do we ask questions?
practice.answer: To learn, to check facts and to get a precise answer so we can act or understand.

practice.question: Which interrogative is missing? ______ is the captain of the netball team?

summary: Who, what, where, when and whose are interrogatives.
Each one asks for a different kind of answer.
A question mark ends the question.

lessons.title: Building questions
objectives: Form questions with who, what, where, when and whose.
Ask a partner about a game or a picture.
lessons.intro: Knowing the five words is only the start. A question has an order. 'Where the field is?' is not yet a finished question. 'Where is the field?' is.
lessons.notes:
### Word order
Many questions follow this pattern:

interrogative + helping verb + subject + rest + ?

Where do you practise?
When does the match start?
What did the captain say?

Who and what can be the subject. Then you do not add do or does:

Who leads the team?
What happened after the whistle?

Whose comes before the thing owned:

Whose kit is this?
Whose name did the coach call?

### Choose the word that matches the gap
Start from the answer and work backwards.

- Answer: Amina. Question: Who scored the last goal?
- Answer: A red ball. Question: What is in the bag?
- Answer: On the field. Question: Where is the match?
- Answer: At four o'clock. Question: When do we meet?
- Answer: The referee's. Question: Whose whistle is on the table?

If the answer is a person, do not begin with where. If the answer is a time, do not begin with whose.

### From a picture or a video
Look at a picture of a game and ask only what you cannot be sure of, or what you want a partner to notice. 'Who is holding the ball?' 'What is the goalkeeper doing?' 'Where is the coach standing?' Keep your voice friendly. A question is not a trap.

Write the questions in your book or type them. Start each one with a capital letter and end with a question mark.

keyWords.meaning: a verb such as is, are, do, does or did that helps to make a question
the order of words in a sentence
the person or thing the sentence is about

examples.problem: Make a question whose answer is 'Behind the stadium'.
steps: The answer is a place.
Begin with where, then the helping verb.

examples.problem: Correct this question: Whose is bottle this?
steps: Whose comes directly before the noun.
The pattern is Whose + noun + verb.

activity.title: Questions from a picture
materials: A picture, cartoon or short video of a game
Exercise books or a shared word processor
steps: View the picture or video together.
Each learner writes five questions, one beginning with who, what, where, when and whose.
Ask a partner your questions. The partner answers in words, not only by pointing.
Type two correct questions, or copy them neatly, and swap books to check capital letters and question marks.

practice.question: Write a where question about a football field.
practice.answer: Example: Where is the football field?

practice.question: Write a when question about athletics practice.
practice.answer: Example: When does athletics practice begin?

practice.question: Correct the order: What the captain did say?
Write a whose question about a kit bag.
practice.answer: Example: Whose kit bag is under the bench?

summary: Begin with the interrogative that matches the answer you want.
Use helping verbs such as do, does and did when the pattern needs them.
Whose sits directly before the thing that is owned.

lessons.title: Answering questions fully
objectives: Give an answer that matches the interrogative.
Answer in a sentence when the situation needs it.
Notice when an answer does not fit the question.
lessons.intro: If someone asks when the race starts and you answer 'On the field', you have named a place. The listener is still late. A useful answer matches the question word.
lessons.notes:
### Match the answer to the word
Listen to the interrogative before you speak.

- Who? Name a person: The captain is Hassan.
- What? Name a thing or an action: We need a ball and a whistle.
- Where? Name a place: We meet on the school field.
- When? Name a time: The match starts at four o'clock.
- Whose? Name an owner: It is the referee's whistle.

A one-word answer can be enough among friends: 'Where is my bottle?' 'Here.' In class, and whenever the listener may not see what you see, answer in a full sentence. 'Your bottle is under the bench.'

### A question-and-answer game
Coach: Who will keep the score?
Asha: I will keep the score.
Coach: What must the players leave at the side?
Juma: They must leave their bags at the side.
Coach: Where is the first-aid box?
Asha: The first-aid box is in the office.
Coach: When do we stop for water?
Juma: We stop for water at half-time.
Coach: Whose turn is it to carry the ball?
Asha: It is my turn.

Each answer uses information from the question. Nobody answers a when question with a person's name.

### If you do not know
It is honest to say, 'I do not know yet.' Then ask someone who does, or look at the notice. Inventing a time or an owner causes confusion. You can also ask for the question to be repeated: 'Could you say the question again, please?'

### Why careful answers matter
Sport depends on shared information. The right person, object, place, time and owner keep a match fair and safe. The same skill helps in every subject: read the question word, then give the kind of fact it asks for.

keyWords.meaning: a sentence with a subject and a verb that can stand alone
the short break in the middle of a match
a box of simple supplies for treating small injuries

examples.problem: The question is 'When is the competition?' Which answer fits: 'Tomorrow morning' or 'The captain'?
steps: When asks for a time.
A person's name does not tell the time.

examples.problem: Turn this short answer into a full sentence. Question: Whose shoes are these? Answer: Amina's.
steps: Repeat the idea of the question.
Include the owner.
examples.answer: These shoes are Amina's. or They are Amina's shoes.

activity.title: Ask and answer in pairs
materials: Question cards for who, what, where, when and whose
steps: Write one sports question for each interrogative on a card.
Swap cards with a partner and answer in full sentences.
Check that the answer matches the question word. If it does not, ask the question again.
Choose your best pair of question and answer and read them to the class.

practice.question: Answer in a full sentence: Where do the players warm up?
practice.answer: Example: The players warm up on the field.

practice.question: A learner answers 'A ball' to the question 'Who is the referee?' What is wrong?
practice.answer: Who asks for a person, but 'a ball' is a thing.

practice.question: Answer: When should you drink water during a match?
practice.answer: Example: You should drink water at half-time or when the coach allows a break.

practice.question: Why should an answer match the interrogative?
practice.answer: So the listener gets the kind of fact they asked for and can act on it.

summary: Who needs a person, what a thing, where a place, when a time and whose an owner.
Use a full sentence when a short answer would be unclear.
Say you do not know rather than inventing a fact.

quiz.question: Which word is an interrogative?
quiz.explanation: Whose is a question word. The others are not interrogatives.

quiz.question: Choose the correct question.
quiz.explanation: Whose comes before the noun: Whose bottle is this?

quiz.question: Which question asks for a place?
Correct the word order of: What the coach did say?
The question is 'Who blew the whistle?' A matching answer is
quiz.explanation: Who needs a person. The referee is a person.

quiz.question: The question is 'When does practice start?' A matching answer is
quiz.explanation: After lunch tells the time. The other answers do not.

quiz.question: Why are interrogatives important?
quiz.answer: They make questions precise so we can learn, check facts and get the right kind of answer.
quiz.explanation: The question word tells everyone what kind of information is needed.

quiz.question: You do not know whose kit is on the bench. What is the best reply?
options: Say you do not know and ask the coach
quiz.explanation: It is honest to admit you do not know and then find out.
